title: Status Code Decision Making
subtopics: Error responses for missing and conflicting resources
Avoiding success responses for failed operations
learning_outcomes: Explain how status code decision making affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from choosing consistent responses to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on status code decision making in http status codes and response headers. You will connect choosing consistent responses to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Status Code Decision Making matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying choosing consistent responses deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Status codes carry protocol-level meaning; headers and structured bodies add metadata needed by clients. In this lesson, treat “Status Code Decision Making” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Status Code Decision Making
content_blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.test/problems/state-conflict",
  "title": "State conflict",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "The order cannot be cancelled after dispatch."
}
content_blocks.expected_output: The status gives generic protocol meaning; problem details explain the application-specific conflict without exposing internal traces.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Choosing consistent responses”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Distinguishing authentication from authorization failures” and “Avoiding success responses for failed operations”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Choose a status from the operation outcome, not from how easy it is to implement. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating status code decision making. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Choosing consistent responses” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.

content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Status Code Decision Making with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating status code decision making as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
